doc.title: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams Interview, 1967-05-13
doc.interviewee: Butch Cage and Robert Pete Williams

chapter: Cage on songs, cane work, records and family
title: Ma Rainey, Memphis Minnie and a woman's blues song
summary: Cage recalls Ma Rainey, seen or confused with another singer, and recites a blues about a woman whose man has left; the interviewer mentions Bessie Smith at Newport and Punch Miller playing the song.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: I'm trying to say something now. I remember Mama Rainey. Oh, yeah.
I like her. Did you ever see her?
No, sir. I saw a lot of them up there, and I forgot what they call her. She's got to play like Mama. She can't get off.
Was she about the same, about as big as Memphis Minnie? Yeah, yeah. About like Memphis Minnie, a big woman? Yeah.
She got on the stage and she saw her.
Did you ever see Memphis Minnie? No. What I see, they shot noises here, a big woman.
Mm-hmm. No, I forgot what they call her. You hear the thing about Mississippi. Weeping Willow Blue. The Weeping Willow?

That's Bessie Smith. I know it. Bessie Smith's like that. I know it. I know it. Bessie Smith's like that. I know it too. Yeah. Her too, huh? Yeah. Where did you see her? What town would that be? That's Newport, Rhode Island. I saw her. Oh, that's late years, huh? Yeah. I saw the one what I'm talkin' bout.
Oh, that's late years, huh? Yeah. I thought it wasn't what I'm talking about. It wasn't Ramping Ma Rainey, but it put him in the mind.

Oh, I know who he's talking about. Is it Mahaney? No, it's a white woman, huh? What's that? Is that a white woman that tries to sing like Ma Rainey in them? No, she was calling. Oh, I don't know who it would be then. Why are there so many of them?

I don't remember that song about if you're broken hearted and your man is out of town, go to the river and jump right up. Take your chance. Take your chance. Take your chance. Make Mennowiller. If he don't come back, let me tell you what to do. Jump right up with boys, cause you ain't no more than you. Cause I thought my man would kiss him morning, noon, and night. I'd wipe you clothes and keep you clean, try to treat him right. Then he went and left me after all I tried to do. The way he treated you, he'd do the same. Mainly he'd do the same to you. I was weeping forever.

I used to play that. I like that. Punch Miller still plays that down in New Orleans. Yes. You might have heard him. He was a solid screen for a long time. Yes. I was born. I ain't been far. Yeah. What about your, uh, back to your family. Now you say your mother was a dancer.
